procedural_history.impugned_order: Order stating that the appellant was not using the property for self-employment to earn a livelihood.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Unknown (not specified in the provided text)
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants appealed to the Supreme Court because they disagreed with the lower court's finding that they were not using the property for self-employment to earn a livelihood, relying on a statement by the first appellant recorded by the Commission.

directions: Set aside the order dated 11.05.2015 passed by the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission in consumer complaint No.276 of 2015.
The complaint is allowed in part.
Respondent to refund sum of Rs.51,10,117/- with interest @ 12% per annum from the date of complaint till date of payment.
Pay litigation cost of Rs. one lakh.

issue.issue_text: Whether the complainant is entitled to a refund of the amount paid towards the office premises, along with interest and litigation costs.

facts: The complainant (appellants) paid a total of Rs. 51,10,117/- to the respondent for an office space.
The respondent failed to deliver possession of the premises within the 24-month period stipulated in the buyer's agreement.
There was no evidence that the office space was ever ready for occupation; the respondent had only offered 'permissive possession'.
The complainant terminated the contract and demanded a refund of the principal amount along with 18% interest and compensation.
The respondent admitted to receiving the principal amount but contended that the complainant had delayed installment payments, for which interest was due.
law: When a seller fails to deliver possession of a property as per the agreement, and the contract is repudiated, the buyer is entitled to a refund of the amount paid.
The court can balance the equities between the parties to arrive at a just and fair resolution, considering the claims and counter-claims of both sides.
application: The Court decided not to send the case back to the lower commission due to the long passage of time (the dispute originated in 2006) and the fact that the contract was already repudiated.
Since executing the sale deed was no longer an option, the Court focused on the complainant's prayer for a refund.
The Court acknowledged the undisputed fact that the respondent had received Rs. 51,10,117/-.
To 'balance the equities', the Court considered both the respondent's failure to deliver the property and their claim that the complainant had delayed payments.

The Court determined that awarding interest at 12% per annum on the principal amount would be fair. This rate was chosen to compensate the complainant for the loss of their money while also offsetting any interest loss the respondent might have incurred due to the complainant's delayed payments.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court partly allowed the complainant's claim. It directed the respondent to refund the entire principal amount of Rs. 51,10,117/-. However, instead of the 18% interest demanded by the complainant, the Court awarded a lower interest rate of 12% per annum to balance the equities between the parties. The claim for litigation costs or other compensation was not explicitly granted in this part of the judgment.

issue.issue_text: Whether the respondent's contention regarding their entitlement to interest on account of delayed payment of instalments by the appellants is tenable.

facts: The respondent (developer) contended that the appellants (buyers) did not pay their instalments on time and were therefore liable to pay interest on the delayed payments.
The appellants had paid a total of ₹51,10,117 to the respondent.
The respondent failed to deliver possession of the office premises within the agreed-upon 24-month period.
The respondent did not plead or provide evidence that the commercial space was ready for occupation.
law: The court has the authority to balance the equities between the parties to ensure a just outcome, especially when there are failures on both sides of an agreement.
application: The Court acknowledged the respondent's claim for interest on delayed payments.
However, it weighed this against the respondent's own significant failure to deliver the property as promised.
To resolve the matter fairly, the Court decided to order a refund of the principal amount paid by the appellants.
The Court further directed the respondent to pay 12% per annum interest on this refunded amount to the appellants.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the respondent's contention for interest by explicitly stating that the 12% interest awarded to the appellants on their refund would serve to "offset the interest loss if at all, if any caused to the respondent on account of delayed payments." This approach balanced the equities, effectively nullifying the respondent's claim in light of their own failure to deliver the property.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the complainant is entitled to a refund of the amount paid towards the office premises, along with interest and litigation costs.
appellant_arguments: The respondent failed to deliver possession of the premises within the agreed-upon 24 months.
The appellants paid a total of Rs. 51,10,117/- towards the premises.
The appellants have repudiated the contract due to the non-delivery and are seeking a refund of the amount paid.
respondent_arguments: The appellants do not qualify as 'consumers' because the office space was not purchased for the purpose of earning a livelihood by way of self-employment.
The respondent offered 'permissive possession' of the premises.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the respondent's contention regarding their entitlement to interest on account of delayed payment of instalments by the appellants is tenable.
appellant_arguments: Any potential interest loss suffered by the respondent due to alleged delayed payments would be offset by the interest awarded to the appellants on the refund amount, especially considering the appreciated value of the property that the respondent retains.
respondent_arguments: The appellants did not remit the instalments on time.
The respondent is entitled to charge interest on the delayed payments.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The explanation added by the Consumer Protection (Amendment) Act 50 of 1993 is clarificatory in nature and applies to all pending proceedings.
obiter: The preamble of the Consumer Protection Act, which was enacted ‘to provide for the protection of the interest of consumers’, furnishes the key to the minds of the makers of the Act and its provisions must be construed in this light.
The definition of 'consumer' is in two parts (goods and services) and uses wide, inclusive expressions to enlarge its ambit, covering not only the purchaser or hirer but also users and beneficiaries.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The appellants qualify as 'consumers' under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, because the pivotal issue is the specific purpose of the transaction, not the general nature of the purchaser's business. The court found that the appellants' statement about being engaged in the business of 'investment/dealing in property' does not ipso facto mean this particular office space was purchased for a 'commercial purpose' of resale. Instead, the court accepted their specific pleading that the space was intended for their own self-employment to run their business and earn a livelihood, thus bringing them under the Act's protection.
legal_tests_applied: Whether the purpose for which a person has bought goods is a 'commercial purpose' within the meaning of the definition of 'consumer' in Section 2(d) of the Consumer Protection Act is a question of fact to be decided in the facts and circumstances of each case.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant won the appeal, and their primary arguments were accepted. However, their complaint was allowed only 'in part' because the court awarded a lower interest rate (12%) and litigation cost (Rs. 1 lakh) than the amounts they had originally demanded in their legal notice (18% interest and Rs. 50,00,00/- compensation). The provided text does not contain the court's specific reasoning for this reduction in the quantum of relief.
policy_considerations: The Consumer Protection Act was enacted 'to provide for the protection of the interest of consumers', and its provisions must be construed in light of this objective.
The Act is intended to help the common person get justice and fair treatment in a market dominated by large entities, especially for wrongs where remedies under ordinary law have become illusory.
The scheme of the Act is to resolve 'business-to-consumer' disputes, not 'business-to-business' disputes, which is a relevant factor in interpreting its definitions and scope.
